quotes.verbatim_quote:
Any guitar may be used for fingerstyle jazz
solo playing—steel string acoustic, nylon
string, or electric. The one requirement is that
both left and right hands have enough room
to finger and pluck without inadvertently
touching and muffling the neighboring strings.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This sets the foundational equipment rule: string spacing is the only non-negotiable criterion for instrument selection.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
The guitar is held in place by the right
elbow, left leg, and the chest. You should
not have to hold it in place with the left hand.
The classical guitar position, with the left
foot raised on a footstool or high stool rung,
is a good model of fingerstyle guitar posture.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Establishes the posture rule that frees the left hand entirely for fretting, a prerequisite for all subsequent technique.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
The traditional symbols for the right hand

fingers are:

Thumb p

Index i

Middle m

Ring a

Pinkie c

c

Left hand fingers are labeled 1, 2, 3, 4, p ima

and T. Separate finger names for each hand
make for easy identification. This means when
you are speaking guitar language, one always
means the first finger of the /eft hand. The
right hand index finger is always called
index, or i (“eye”).
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines the notation vocabulary used throughout the entire book; misreading these symbols would make every fingering instruction unintelligible.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
The thumb p of the right hand points out toward
the left in an inverted hitch-hiking position. This
creates space between the thumb and index finger
so that they won't run into each other.

Tilt the first three fingers back (toward the bridge)
so that they are in line when you place them all ona
single string. On the rare occasions when you need
to use the pinkie c, the hand lowers so that all of the
fingers are in line.

Keep the back of the hand arched —at least level
with the plane of the strings, if not higher.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Specifies three interlocking rules (thumb angle, finger tilt, arch height) that together produce the ergonomically correct right-hand shape for all fingerstyle strokes.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
To emphasize a melody, use a volume producing technique called the rest stroke. To play a rest
stroke, place your guitar, arm, and hand in the position described above. Temporarily rest the thumb
lightly on the sixth string away from the other fingers. Hover the index i, middle m, and ring finger a,
directly in front of the first string. Keeping the finger supple and not frozen, pluck the first string with
the left side of the fingertip and nail — if you have nails — and come to rest on the adjacent second
string. Now play the same stroke on the first string with the m finger, while simultaneously lifting the
ifinger away from its temporarily parked position on the second string.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This is the method's primary melody-projection technique and the first full procedural description of how to execute the fundamental stroke.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
When you pluck, do not rest the plucking finger on the string to be plucked. Instead, momentarily
hover the finger in front of the string to be plucked. Start swinging the finger before you meet the
string to be struck, just as you would in baseball, tennis, or handball. It takes courage, because you
may first swipe at and miss the string, or strike more strings than you intend. Striking while in motion
is especially important when you are about to pluck an already ringing string, because if you rest
even for a second, you will damp (truncate) the previous note and interrupt the flow of sound
between notes.
quotes.why_load_bearing: States the critical rule against pre-resting the finger and explains precisely why doing so kills legato flow, naming the exact failure mode it prevents.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
If you have smooth, oval-shaped fingernails on
every finger, or nonails protruding beyond the fingertips, you are in good shape. If you have a mix
of uneven nails on some fingers and no nails on others, you need to file them all down to the same
length and let them grow out at the same rate. On your left hand you should have nails as short
as possible.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Sets the maintenance standard for nails on both hands, which directly affects tone consistency across all right-hand fingers.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Right-hand stroking with alternating iand m fingers (i-m) is the way to produce a fluent flow
of notes. This alternating finger technique is like walking by putting one foot in front of the other.
Using just one plucking finger would be like trying to walk by hopping on one foot.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Establishes alternating i-m as the foundational fluency mechanism and provides the kinesthetic analogy that justifies the rule.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Often fingers of
the left hand need to be on the “tip toes of
the fingertips” to avoid blocking the adja-
cent strings. Arching the wrist outward helps
accomplish this finger action.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Gives the key left-hand technique cue that prevents inadvertent string muting in chord voicings and melody playing.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
The ball of the left thumb should be well
under the neck of the instrument, working in
opposition to the fingers on the fretboard. In
some instances the thumb is used to play
bass notes on the sixth string, but it should
not be hooked around the neck in anticipa-
tion of these movements, as it will inhibit
other more prevalent movements and
stretches.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines the default thumb position and explicitly forbids the wraparound habit, explaining the mechanical cost of violating the rule.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
When notes occur in a repeated pattern across the same set of strings, right hand fingers may
be assigned one finger per string to match this pattern. This is particularly true in three finger/three
string combinations

In the next exercise the a finger takes care of the first string, m plays the second string, and /

plays the third.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Introduces the second major picking scheme as a complement to alternation, governing how the right hand handles arpeggiated and cross-string patterns.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
When the notes stay on one
string, use a steady alternating pair such as i-m. Determine whether it would make any difference
if you started the exercise with m rather than i. If the notes are making a repeated pattern across
several strings, assign one finger per string. Don’t become too obsessive about the ultimate
correct fingering choices. In realistic situations you would alternate between both systems as you
need.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Synthesizes both picking systems into a practical decision rule students can apply independently when choosing their own fingering.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Hover the thumb above the sixth string. Move it in a
down and forward movement , striking the sixth string with the lower, outer edge of the thumb tip and
nail. Clear the fifth string by arcing upward in a circular movement and returning to the starting
position. If you have a very straight thumb, you may instead flick the first tip segment toward the area
underneath your palm, then returning to starting position. You are making a free stroke, which does
not touch an adjacent string. Generally the thumb does not use the rest stroke as it can easily
overpower the melody being played with the i, m, or a fingers.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Gives the complete procedural description of the thumb free stroke and states the critical rule against using rest stroke with the thumb to protect melodic balance.
